Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 118 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 118 is 
located in southeast AB, south of the Cypress Hills 
Interprovincial Park boundary and north of secondary 
highway 501. This WMU is dominated by native dry 
mixed-grass prairie with extensive silver sagebrush 
communities. It also contains numerous permanent 
and intermittent watercourses forming sinuous steep to 
rolling valley complexes. The majority of the WMU 
contains very little tree cover. It is considered one of 
the premier mule deer units in Alberta due to it being 
dominated by large blocks of high-quality native 
habitat with relatively low human impacts. Land 
ownership is dominated by provincially owned Public 
Land under grazing lease, and cattle ranching is the 
primary human land use in the area. The total area of 
the WMU is 1964 km2.
Chr onic Wasting Disease is now well established 
within the WMU, with 68 positives since first detected 
in 2013 (https://open.alberta.ca/publications/chronic-
wasting-disease-in-alberta-by-wildlife-management-
unit) . Submitted samples from 2023 indicate 
prevalence rates of 18% in mule deer and 19% of 21 
mule deer bucks tested positive for the disease. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, 
elk, and moose) was last conducted for WMU 118 in 
2018-19 using the distance survey methodology 
(Table 1). With 5 years since the last survey, an 
updated population estimate is needed to ensure 
management goals are based on more relevant data. 
It is important to consider the difference in methods 
when comparing results between the surveys.  
The objective of the February 2025 survey was to 
assess the status of the deer and moose populations 
in WMU 118 by determining estimates for abundance, 
density and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including elk, 
pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at-
risk species. 
S
urvey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 8–11, 2025 flying 31 east-west 
lines at 1.85 km intervals, with 49.7% coverage (800 m 
wide survey strip, area surveyed 975 km2) for a total 
linear survey effort of 1219 km. At each observation 
point, ungulates were classified by species, and when 
possible, sex and age were recorded. Antler size for 
deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on 
one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more 
points; antlers inside ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 
points, antlers outside of ears). 
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose 
was calculated by multiplying the number of animals 
per transect (∑x) by total area (km2) searched (total 
survey strip area [∑z]) (Jolly 1969, as described in 
Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with 90% confidence intervals. Confidence 
interval width was calculated by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-
distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq 
root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-
1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number 
of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as 
the number of transects sampled. 
Elk observations were recorded as a minimum total 
count (MTC) within the WMU.  
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 985 mule deer were observed with an 
average groups size of 15 (range 1-57). The estimated 
density was 1.01 mule deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 1,983 individuals (90% CI 1,419 – 
2,547). A total of 881 mule deer were successfully 
classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated 
to be 26:100:67. That results in an estimated 2024/25 
winter mule deer population of 267 bucks, 1028 does, 
and 688 fawns. Of the 118 mule deer bucks classified,

26 (22%) were classified ‘small’, 38 (32%) ‘medium’, 
and 54 (46%) ‘large’. The 2024 population estimate 
represents a 14.5% decrease from the last aerial 
ungulate survey population estimate for mule deer 
within WMU 118 (conducted in 2018/19). The survey 
in 2024/25 also showed a large decrease in the buck 
to doe ratio. It should be noted that several one-
antlered bucks were observed indicating antler drop 
was underway, and buck numbers were undoubtedly 
underrepresented in the totals. The fawn to doe ratio 
was consistent between surveys suggesting stable 
reproduction rates in the population (Table 1). When 
comparing survey results, it is important to note that 
the last survey used a different survey methodology 
(Distance vs Transect).  
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 36 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 6 (range 2-11). The estimated 
density was 0.037 deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 72 individuals (90% CI 36 – 109). Due 
to the small sample of white-tailed deer detected in 
this survey, classification data was unable to be 
compiled. Furthermore, it is likely the majority of antler 
shed had occurred in white-tailed deer, as this was the 
case in adjacent WMUs. White-tail numbers in the 
neighboring management unit 116 also increased 
dramatically from the previous year, suggesting winter 
movements between units that impact abundance 
estimates.  
Incidental observations 
A total of 16 moose were observed with an average 
group size of 3 (range 1-8). The estimated density was 
0.016 moose/km2 and the estimated abundance was 
32 individuals (90% CI 11 – 53). Moose were generally 
confined to brushy creek valleys and associated 
coulees as suitable moose habitat is generally limited 
in prairie WMUs.  
Other species observed included 166 elk, sharp-tailed 
grouse, gray partridge, porcupine, and coyote.  
WMU 624 (Cypress Hills Provincial Park) was also 
surveyed during the WMU 118 survey. A total of 14 
mule deer, 11 White-tailed deer, four elk, and four 
moose were observed within the park. The small 
samples obtained from Cypress Hills did not provide 
enough data for a population estimation for this WMU. 
It is likely the deep snow conditions in the park in 2025 
had caused most ungulates to leave and move to 
lower elevations where they were captured by the 
surveys in surrounding WMUs.
